A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the use of noninvasive methods for the assessment of liver fibrosis is feasible in patients with hepatitis c virus (HCV)/human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) co-infection.
we have shown that the noninvasive assessment of liver fibrosis in HCV/HIV patients can be improved by using a combination of noninvasive methods and by taking the HIV viral load into consideration.
we have shown that the combination of the two methods of liver stiffness measurement, transient elastography and MR elastography, can be used to assess liver fibrosis in HCV/HIV co-infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is no evidence of increased risk of liver disease progression in patients with HCV/HIV coinfection who have achieved sustained virologic response to HCV treatment compared to those who have not.

we have identified a new mechanism for the pathogenesis of liver fibrosis and that it is likely to be a general mechanism in the pathogenesis of many forms of liver fibrosis, not just in the context of HCV infection.
there are a variety of non-invasive methods for assessing the degree of fibrosis and cirrhosis, which is important for determining the prognosis and treatment of patients with chronic hepatitis C.
